In this video, you'll learn what plugins are, what's inside them, how to install and share them, and how to build your very own — step by step.
Let's begin with a simple question: why do we need plugins at all?
Without plugins, every person sets up Claude on their own. Custom commands, helper agents, tool connections, and automation rules live in scattered files, and they're hard to share with a team.
With plugins, all of that is packaged into one bundle. You install it with a single command, and everyone on the team gets the exact same setup — instantly.
Plugins turn your best Claude workflows into something you can share, reuse, and keep up to date.
So, what exactly is a Claude plugin?
A plugin is a package that extends Claude with new capabilities. It's simply a folder, with a standard structure that Claude knows how to read.
At its heart is a small manifest file, called plugin dot json, which gives the plugin its name, version, and description.
Around it sit the components: folders for commands, agents, and skills, plus optional files for hooks and MCP servers.
Install the folder, and Claude instantly gains everything inside it. Turn it off, and it's gone — clean and simple.
A plugin can contain several types of components. Let's look at each one.
Slash commands are shortcuts you type, like slash review or slash close checklist. Each command is a Markdown file with instructions for Claude.
Subagents are specialized assistants with their own focus and tools — for example, a code reviewer, or a reconciliation agent.
Skills are packages of know-how that Claude loads automatically, whenever a task needs them.
Hooks are automatic rules that run at key moments — for example, running a check every time a file is edited.
MCP servers connect Claude to external tools and data, such as a database, a CRM, or a design tool.
And the manifest ties everything together into one installable package.
You might be wondering how plugins relate to features you may already know.
Think of the plugin as the bundle — the box that holds everything, ready to install and share.
Skills are the know-how inside it: instructions Claude follows for specific tasks.
MCP servers are the connections: they give Claude access to outside tools and data.
And hooks are the guardrails: automatic actions that keep work consistent and safe.
In short, a plugin can package skills, MCP connections, hooks, commands, and agents — all together.
Let's open a plugin and look at its structure.
Every plugin has a hidden folder called dot claude plugin, which holds the manifest file, plugin dot json.
The manifest gives the plugin its identity: a unique name, a version number, a short description, and the author.
Next to it, components live in standard folders — commands, agents, and skills — so Claude finds them automatically.
Hooks are defined in a hooks file, and MCP servers in a dot MCP dot json file. That's the whole structure.
Where do plugins come from? They're shared through marketplaces.
A marketplace is a catalog of plugins. Technically, it's just a repository with a marketplace file that lists each plugin and where to find it.
Anthropic offers official plugins, so you can get started right away.
Your company can host its own private marketplace, with plugins built for your team.
And the community shares many more — though you should always check that a source is trustworthy before installing.
Now let's install a plugin in Claude Code. It only takes a few steps.
First, add a marketplace, using the slash plugin marketplace add command, followed by the repository name.
Second, install the plugin you want, with slash plugin install.
Third, open the slash plugin menu at any time, to browse, enable, or disable your plugins.
And finally, start using it. The new commands, agents, and skills are available right away.
Plugins aren't only for developers. In Claude Cowork, Anthropic offers ready-made plugins designed for different roles.

There are plugins for sales, finance, legal, and marketing teams — each with commands and skills for that job, like preparing a call, reconciling accounts, reviewing a contract, or planning a campaign.
There are also plugins for data analysis, customer support, product management, and everyday productivity.
Each plugin can connect to the tools that team already uses, and organizations can customize them to fit their own processes.
Let's see a plugin in action. Imagine a finance team, using a month-end close plugin.
Step one: the plugin is installed once, for the whole team.
Step two: Claude loads its components — the commands, agents, skills, and connections.
Step three: an accountant types a command, like slash close checklist.
Step four: a specialized agent follows the plugin's skills, and uses MCP connections to pull data from the accounting system.
And step five: hooks run automatic checks, and the team gets a consistent, reviewable result.
Let's take a closer look at hooks, because they're one of the most powerful parts of a plugin.
Each hook listens for an event. For example, post tool use fires right after Claude uses a tool. Other events include pre tool use, session start, and stop.
A matcher decides which tools the hook applies to — here, whenever Claude edits or writes a file.
The action is a command that runs automatically — in this example, a linter that checks the code.
The result: important checks happen every single time, without anyone having to remember them.
Ready to build your own plugin? Here's how, in four steps.
First, create a folder for your plugin, with a dot claude plugin folder and a plugin dot json manifest inside.
Second, add your components — for example, a commands folder with a Markdown file for each slash command.
Third, test it locally. Load your plugin in Claude Code, and try every command and agent.
And fourth, publish it. Add it to a marketplace, so your team — or the world — can install it with a single command.
Plugins can be shared at different levels, depending on who needs them.
Level one is personal. You install plugins for yourself, to speed up your own work.
Level two is the project or team. A repository can list recommended marketplaces and plugins in its settings, so every teammate gets the same tools.
Level three is the whole organization. Admins can manage private marketplaces, and control which plugins are available to everyone.
This way, the best workflows spread across the company — safely and consistently.
Before we wrap up, here are six best practices for using plugins.
One: install plugins only from marketplaces you trust.
Two: review what's inside, because hooks and MCP servers can run code on your machine.
Three: keep each plugin focused on one clear purpose.
Four: use version numbers and a changelog, so everyone knows what changed.
Five: write clear descriptions for every command, agent, and skill.
And six: disable plugins you're not using, to keep Claude fast and focused.
Let's recap in one line: package, install, share.
Claude plugins bundle commands, agents, skills, hooks, and connections — turning your best workflows into tools that everyone can use.
